# Tkinter

Python's standard-library GUI toolkit. Chosen in both lab repositories for the same stated reason:
it ships with Python, so a marker can run the program without installing anything.

## Nim game — Discrete Maths lab 4

A four-variant Nim implementation with an AI opponent, see [[sprague-grundy-nim-sum]]. The structure
is worth recording independently of the toolkit:

- **Layered**: variants → players → state → screens. The game rules never touch a widget, so the same
  engine drives all four variants.
- **Screens instantiated once, raised with `tkraise()`** rather than destroyed and rebuilt on
  navigation. Widget state survives, and there is no rebuild cost or stale-callback risk from
  tearing down frames.

`PROJECT.md` defends the choice only as "no external UI dependencies".
**TODO:** whether PyQt, pygame or a web UI were considered, or stdlib-only was a hard course
constraint, is not recorded. `confidence: low` on the rationale.

## Knowledge browser — Python labs 13/14

A [[sqlite]]-backed browser over a 610-row corpus, in [[python-programming-laboratories]]. Two
choices that generalise past Tkinter:

- **Listbox rows are mapped by index to their record**, never by parsing the displayed label back
  into data. Parsing your own UI text is the bug that appears the moment a label contains a
  separator character.
- The database **connection is opened in `main()` and closed by `contextlib.closing`**, not opened at
  import — the same boundary discipline as [[separating-computation-from-io]].

## Where it sits among the alternatives

Both uses are desktop apps that had to be handed in and run. Compare the browser-based deliverables in
the same Discrete Maths repo — [[offline-first-static-deliverable]] — which solve the "runs
anywhere with no install" problem with an HTML file instead. Tkinter wins when the program is Python
and must stay Python; the HTML route wins when it must open on a machine with no interpreter.
